title: Why Your Prompts Get Average Answers

segments.say:
Welcome to Prompt Engineering Masterclass, module 1, lesson 1: Why Your Prompts Get Average Answers.

You already use ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Sometimes the answer is brilliant. And sometimes it's generic, too long, or quietly wrong. In this lesson, we'll look at why that happens, and we'll set up the mindset you'll use for the rest of the course.

segments.title: Why AI answers disappoint
bullets: A chat assistant is a prediction engine
It produces the most likely helpful continuation
Short, vague prompt - it fills gaps with the average
Average is rarely what clients or managers want
segments.say: Let's start with the real reason AI answers disappoint. A chat assistant is a prediction engine. It reads everything you give it and produces the most likely helpful continuation. So when your prompt is short and vague, the model fills the gaps with the most average answer it can think of. And here's the thing: average is rarely what a client, a manager or an examiner wants.

segments.title: Priya's first attempt
bullets: Three cheerful paragraphs, 5 emojis, 11 hashtags
Not wrong - just not hers
AI didn't know it's a jaggery and millet cake
Missed the brand voice, 60-word limit, Sunday offer
segments.note: Prompt: "Write an Instagram post about our new cake."
segments.say:
Let's look at an example. Priya is a marketing executive at a Pune bakery chain. She types a simple request. Here's the prompt: "Write an Instagram post about our new cake."

She gets three cheerful paragraphs, five emojis and eleven hashtags. It's not wrong. It's just not hers. The AI didn't know the cake is a jaggery and millet cake for health-conscious customers. It didn't know the brand voice is warm but never cheesy, that posts must be under sixty words, or that the offer ends Sunday.

segments.title: Priya's second attempt
bullets: Role: social media writer for Crumb and Co.
Voice: warm, understated, max two emojis
Audience: health-conscious Pune families, 28-45
Facts: no refined sugar, Rs 450 for 500 g, MILLET10
Under 60 words, 5 hashtags, 3 options
segments.quote: Nothing magical happened. Priya simply stopped making the model guess.
segments.say:
Now compare that with her second attempt. This time, Priya tells the AI it's the social media writer for Crumb and Co., a Pune bakery known for warm, understated writing, with no exclamation marks and a maximum of two emojis. She asks for an Instagram caption launching the Jaggery Millet Cake. She names the audience, health-conscious families in Pune aged twenty-eight to forty-five. She lists the key facts: no refined sugar, made with ragi and jowar, four hundred and fifty rupees for five hundred grams. She gives the offer, ten percent off till Sunday with the code MILLET10. She sets the length, under sixty words, then five relevant hashtags on a new line. And she asks for three options with different opening lines. You'll find the full prompt in the lesson notes below this video.

Same model, same day, very different result. Nothing magical happened. Priya simply stopped making the model guess.

segments.title: Specification, not trickery
bullets: Forget secret phrases and "prompt hacks"
Write a clear brief, like briefing a new team member
Professional prompting is less mysterious than it looks
segments.quote: If a smart intern would need to ask five questions, your prompt is missing five pieces of information.
segments.say: That brings us to an important idea. Prompt engineering is specification, not trickery. Lots of online "prompt hacks" promise secret phrases. In practice, professional prompt engineering is much less mysterious. It's the skill of writing a clear brief, the way a good manager briefs a new team member. Here's a useful test. If a smart intern who'd never met you would need to ask five questions before starting, your prompt is missing five pieces of information.

segments.title: Four common failure patterns
grid: Generic answer - say who, for whom, and why
Wrong length or tone - state the rules
Wall of text - ask for a table, bullets, JSON
Shallow answer - break it into steps
segments.say: There are four common failure patterns, and the lesson notes have them in a table. First, missing context. That gives you a generic, could-be-anyone answer, and the fix is to say who, for whom, and why. Second, missing constraints. The answer is too long, in the wrong tone, or the wrong format, so you state the length, the tone, and what it must and must not do. Third, missing format. You get a wall of text you have to reformat, so you ask for a table, bullets, or JSON. And fourth, too much at once. A big task gets a shallow answer, so you break it into steps. You'll learn a fix for each of these in the coming lessons.

segments.title: What "expert results" mean
numbered: Relevant - fits your exact situation
Reliable - ten runs, ten usable answers
Ready to use - right format, minimal editing
Honest - admits when it doesn't know
Reusable - saved, shared, still works
segments.quote: A prompt that works once is a toy. A prompt that works every Monday is a tool.
segments.say:
So what do "expert results" actually mean? By the end of this course, you should be able to get output with five qualities. First, it's relevant. It addresses your exact situation, not a textbook version of it. Second, it's reliable. Run the prompt ten times and you get ten usable answers, not three. Third, it's ready to use, with the correct format, the correct length, and minimal editing. Fourth, it's honest. The model tells you when it doesn't know, instead of inventing facts. And fifth, it's reusable. The prompt can be saved, shared with a colleague, and it still works.

Reliability is the one most casual users never think about. A prompt that works once in a lucky chat is a toy. A prompt that works every Monday for your whole team is a tool.

segments.title: Model-agnostic thinking
bullets: Works across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot
Features change often - principles transfer
Tool-specific features described generally
segments.note: Habit: run the same prompt in two assistants and compare.
segments.say:
Next, let's talk about model-agnostic thinking. This course works across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and most other chat assistants. Each tool has its own strengths, and their features change often, so we focus on principles that transfer. When a feature is tool-specific, like Custom GPTs or Claude Projects, we describe it generally, so you can find the equivalent in whichever tool your company uses.

Here's one practical habit. Keep two assistants open while you learn, and run the same prompt in both. You'll quickly see that a well-structured prompt produces good results everywhere, while a vague prompt produces vague results everywhere.

segments.title: Five modules
numbered: Foundations: anatomy, examples, delimiters, templates
Controlling output: reasoning, formats, refinement
Reliability: hallucinations, chaining, testing
Real work: writing, analysis, extraction, code, images
Scaling up: assistants, team library, safe use
segments.say: Now, here's how this course works. There are five modules. Module one is Foundations: the anatomy of a prompt, examples, delimiters and templates. Module two is about controlling output: reasoning, structured formats, and refinement. Module three is about reliability: reducing hallucinations, chaining, and testing prompts. Module four covers prompts for real work: writing, analysis, data extraction, coding, and images. And module five is about scaling up: custom assistants, a team prompt library, and safe use.

segments.title: Four portfolio projects
grid: Built for a specific job role
segments.note: Prompting is hands-on, like driving. Do every exercise.
segments.say: Every lesson ends with a short exercise. Do them. Prompting is a hands-on skill, like driving. Reading about it only helps a little. Along the way, you'll build four portfolio projects you can show on LinkedIn or in an interview. A twenty-five prompt professional library. A chain that turns meeting notes into a report. A tested data-extraction prompt. And a custom assistant for a job role.

segments.title: Start a Prompt Journal
segments.say: Before we get to the exercise, start a prompt journal. Create a simple document or spreadsheet called "Prompt Journal", with six columns: the date, the task, the prompt itself copied and pasted, the tool you used, a result quality score from one to five, and what you'd change. The exact layout is in the lesson notes. Every time a prompt works really well or fails badly, log it. Within a few weeks, this becomes the raw material for your personal prompt library in module five.

segments.title: Try it yourself · 15 minutes
numbered: Pick a real task from your work or studies
Write your usual prompt, run it, save the output
Rewrite it: who, what, facts, length, tone, format
Run the new prompt, then in a second tool
Score all three outputs 1-5 in your Prompt Journal
segments.note: Ask: who is it for, what exactly, which facts, how long, what tone, what format?
segments.say:
Now it's your turn. Try it yourself. Spend about fifteen minutes on this, and feel free to pause the video while you work.

Step one. Pick a real task from your work or studies this week. An email, a summary, a lesson plan, or a LinkedIn post.

Step two. Write the prompt the way you normally would. Run it, and save the output.

Step three. Now rewrite the prompt, answering these questions inside it. Who is this for? What exactly do I want? What facts must be included? How long? What tone? And what format?

segments.title: Try it yourself · 15 minutes
numbered: Pick a real task from your work or studies
Write your usual prompt, run it, save the output
Rewrite it: who, what, facts, length, tone, format
Run the new prompt, then in a second tool
Score all three outputs 1-5 in your Prompt Journal
segments.note: Note the single change that made the biggest difference.
segments.say:
Step four. Run the new prompt in the same tool. Then run it in a second tool.

Step five. Compare all three outputs and score each one from one to five in your new Prompt Journal. Note the single change that made the biggest difference.

Go ahead and pause now if you'd like to do that.

segments.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Vague prompts get average answers
Prompting is clear specification, not secret phrases
Aim for relevant, reliable, ready, honest, reusable
Good principles transfer across all assistants
Start your Prompt Journal today
segments.say:
Let's recap. Vague prompts get average answers, because the model fills every gap with the most typical guess. Prompt engineering is clear specification, like briefing a smart new colleague, not secret phrases. Aim for answers that are relevant, reliable, ready to use, honest and reusable. Good prompting principles transfer across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other assistants. And start your Prompt Journal today, because it becomes your professional prompt library later.

That's it for this lesson. Mark it complete, and I'll see you in the next one.
